name: Cypress, real sites
q: Do filed plans meet at today's approximate sites?
r: Almost never at today's spacing (0 planned conflicts in 20 h without Amazon).

name: Houston build-out density
q: How do planned conflicts grow as sites fill in?
r: With the square of site density; Amazon in about 90 % of planned conflicts.

name: Height allocation
q: Can heights inside each filed band separate the operators?
r: About 80 % fewer planned conflicts against the filed heights (re-measured: 81 %, 92 %). Against the high-return case (122 m back, staff remark only), only 23 % (see Pre-launch robustness).

name: Free spread vs allocation
q: Is spreading heights freely as good as allocating them?
r: No: free spread cut 19–32 %, allocation 80 %+.

name: Robustness
q: Does the allocation hold across thresholds and peak hours?
r: Holds for 15–50 m thresholds and the busiest hour; at 20 m vertical separation it cut more than predicted (58–59 %). Its Dallas–Fort Worth figure (50–54 %) came from an older counter that checked once a second; rerun on the current counter with the same company mix, the cut is 75 % (77 % with Houston's Amazon share), in line with 78 % on the real DFW layout (exploratory rerun, 27 Oct 2026).

name: Procedures near sites
q: What removes the remaining planned conflicts?
r: A shared plan check removes all, delaying 1.5–4.8 % of flights. 3 predictions not scored (a pre-run check failed).

name: Profile shape vs priority rule
q: Why is Amazon delayed most?
r: Climbing in place did not fix it; priority rules move delay without removing it.

name: Vertical speed
q: Do Amazon's slow climbs cause its delays?
r: No: faster climbs cut crossing time 71 % but delays only 31–44 %.

name: Equal fleet sizes
q: Is it fleet size instead?
r: Mostly: equal fleets shrink the gap by about 70 %.

name: Richardson no-fly zone
q: Does the hospital no-fly zone explain one home's overflights?
r: It funnels traffic 3–4× but explains about a fifth of the count.

name: Reserved volume size
q: What does each flight's reserved airspace cost?
r: Delay roughly proportional to width; a 20 m vertical gap costs about 5×.

name: Surge and pop-up restriction
q: How do a 3× surge and a pop-up no-fly zone play out?
r: Surge doubles delayed share, recovers within 30 min; restriction mainly holds flights.

name: Off-plan drones (allocation)
q: Do stopped or landing drones meet other companies?
r: Too rare to compare (4 in 4,838).

name: Off-plan drones (filed heights)
q: Does the allocation help when drones go off-plan?
r: Yes against filed heights (9.4× fewer per stop); in the high-return case (staff remark) only 1.4× [0.8–2.4].

name: Return-to-home and outage
q: Does a common return height matter?
r: Return at 120 m is about 10.7× riskier than at own height (corrected).

name: Area outages
q: Is freezing together riskier, or being caught mid-climb?
r: Filed heights 7× riskier than allocation (1-per-second counting). Not yet re-measured for the high-return case.

name: Counting fix and re-runs
q: Do the headline numbers survive finer counting and error ranges?
r: Yes: 81 % [78–84], 92 % [89–95]; contingency ratios corrected down.

name: Wing at fixed heights
q: Does the allocation depend on how Wing picks its height?
r: No: 81–84 % cut at 46, 61, 76 m and random.

name: Pre-launch robustness
q: Does the result survive Amazon's real heights, height error and other layouts?
r: Lifting Amazon's return 10 m+ removes ~75 % on its own; then allocation adds 23 %. Height error 3/5 m: 72/63 %. 30 layouts: 83 %. 6 km was not weaker (prediction failed).

name: Bad days, high-return case
q: Do the bad-day and delay benefits hold against Amazon's reported heights?
r: Mostly not: holds 1.4× [0.8–2.4], delay 1.3×. Nearly all came from the 4 m Amazon–Zipline gap.

name: Houston today, real sites
q: Do the sites flying today in Houston meet?
r: 1-2 planned conflicts in 60 h at the filed caps, none at 20 %: Amazon and Zipline are too far apart.

name: Real Houston layout
q: Real Amazon sites, full filed site counts
r: Cut 79 % (Omaha profile), 71 % (Texas band), 27 % (high-return case); 3 seeds, superseded by HEADLINE2.

name: Real DFW layout
q: Same with Amazon's six geocoded DFW sites
r: Cut 76 / 67 / 3 % with 3 seeds; 10 seeds gave 80 / 73 / 33 % (SEEDS).

name: Customers where people live
q: Census 2020 population weighting
r: Headline unchanged (77 / 71 / 23 %).

name: Amazon best-sourced heights
q: Amazon 69 m out, back anywhere in 85-115 m
r: 71 % Houston, 66 % DFW (3 seeds; see HEADLINE2).

name: Shared departure paths
q: Do departure corridors explain Richardson's overflights?
r: About two shared paths reproduce it (a fit, not proof); headline unchanged.

name: Real wind
q: Does Houston and DFW wind change the result?
r: Height sharing 72-84 % across wind bands; a plan check with no wind allowance fails in wind.

name: Build-out stages
q: Today to full build-out, Houston and DFW
r: 0 / 0.5 / 6.3 / 36 an hour (Houston), 0.5 / 3.0 / 25 (DFW); most involve Amazon and Zipline.

name: More seeds
q: 10 seeds instead of 3
r: Cuts stable (81-83 % Houston, 80 % DFW); DFW high-return cut 33 %, not 3 %.

name: Real Walmart sites
q: Wing grows onto real stores
r: Little change against random sites (cuts 72-80 %).

name: Fixed pads
q: Pads with occupancy at sites
r: 86-99 % fewer near-site conflicts than random pads; Zipline Houston needs more than 20 docks.

name: DFW bad days and plan-check cost
q: Bad-day tests and check cost with the DFW mix
r: Hover sharing 7.6x; common return height 5.9x worse; 1-2 % of flights delayed shared out.

name: Drones near an air-taxi site (VTXPAD)
q: Drones near Toyota's Plano HQ at full DFW build-out
r: About 19 an hour within 1 km (range 7-51 over layouts), about 6 within 300 m.

name: Amazon at today's volume
q: Amazon at 20 % of cap (about 200 a day)
r: Conflicts fall about two thirds; Amazon still about 80 % of what remains; sharing out cuts 79 % DFW, 62 % Houston.

name: Headline rerun (review fixes)
q: 10 runs, bounded counting, stricter separation rules
r: 72 % Houston [67-76], 73 % DFW [66-80]; 55 % / 45 % if 15 m is needed; 29 % / 35 % in the high-return case.

name: Air taxis near take-off sites
q: Drones near air-taxi climb-outs and approaches (both metros)
r: None today at the TMC helipad; at full build-out about 2 in 5 movements (Houston) and 1 in 3 (DFW) with a drone inside well clear on planned paths, 1 in 20 to 1 in 45 inside NMAC. Drones yielding to booked air-taxi movements removes all for about one 2-minute delay per movement.

name: Realistic plan sharing (COORD1)
q: Reserved volumes inspired by ASTM F3548 (standard not read; sizes assumed), plans made on an hour-old wind forecast
r: Flown conflicts cut 96–99 %; about 1 flight in 5 (Houston) or 6 (DFW) waits, about 6 minutes on average, with this project's shared-out heights in windy hours (I predicted at most 5 % delayed); the old ±5 s check leaves half the conflicts in wind. 14–15 % of flights leave their reserved windows.

name: Layer gaps sized to the reservation (COORD2)
q: Do 20 m gaps between company layers cut the cost of coordination?
r: Delays fall by about 60 % (Houston 19 % to 8 %, DFW 17 % to 7 %); Amazon still waits most, because it climbs through every layer.

name: Coordination cost vs demand (DENS1)
q: A quarter to twice the filed demand
r: Uncoordinated conflicts grow steeply with demand (fitted exponent 1.65–2.4; my 1.7–2.3 prediction failed narrowly); with the shared-out heights the delayed share stays near 20 % while cancellations rise; gap-sized layers are cheaper at every demand level.

name: Air-taxi engine vs a published vertiport model (VERTIPORT1)
q: Does the air-taxi engine reproduce Vascik & Hansman (MIT, AIAA SciTech 2019)?
r: Yes, for one pad with 1-8 stands: pad use within 10 points of theirs in 15 of 16 cases and the same saturation points; it falls up to 15 points short where their optimised schedule beats first-come first-served. Setting it up showed engine versions 1-3 never let full stands block a landing; version 4 fixes this.

name: Order of the height layers (LAYER1)
q: Does putting Zipline on top of the layers cut conflicts and delay?
r: It cuts flown conflicts by about 40 % (Amazon-Zipline 39 to 8 in Houston) but not coordination delay: with layers 12 m apart and reserved blocks 10 m thick, cruising flights in neighbouring layers still block each other on paper. Order and gap-versus-block thickness are separate levers.

name: Layer order plus thinner reserved blocks (LAYER2)
q: Zipline on top and 5 m blocks instead of 10 m, together
r: Delayed flights fall from 18.5 % to 4.4 % (Houston) and 17.0 % to 4.1 % (DFW); Amazon from 83 % to 26 % and 80 % to 18 %; flown conflicts no higher than with 10 m blocks (counts too small to show a difference). Thinner blocks do most of it; order adds a further 44 % only once blocks are thin. Whether 5 m blocks are safe is not tested.

name: Who could save time flying between Archer's sites (ACCESS1)
q: Census blocks and commute flows: how many existing commuters would cut 10+ minutes door to door?
r: Under generous road-speed assumptions 2.6 % of DFW and 1.2 % of Houston jobs (87,000 and 34,000) would save 10+ minutes, mostly long cross-metro commutes (about 67-77 km against a typical 20 km); off peak 0.3-0.4 %. No income skew (a prediction that failed). Slower local access roads cut this to 0.2-0.3 %. Adding Archer's last two sites (addendum): Frisco Station raises DFW to 3.1 %; the downtown Houston helipad puts about 730,000 more people within 15 minutes of a site but adds almost no time-savers, because downtown is a short drive from Hobby. Counts people with a time saving, not riders: fares, capacity and weather are not modelled.

name: Parking stands per air-taxi site (STANDS1)
q: How many stands does each site need once full stands block landings (engine v4)?
r: The registered test failed for a reason unrelated to stands: v4 makes arriving aircraft wait briefly for a pad, and with no charge margin any wait dips below the 20-minute reserve. Without that test (exploratory): about 4 stands per site at the lowest demand and 5-6 at the next; the 6 used since NET1 work in 7 of 10 seeds there; at higher demand the 2 pads run out before the stands do (DFW from 6 requests an hour per route direction, Houston from 12). Next: an arrival-priority pad rule.

name: Landing rule with limited stands (PADRULE1)
q: Does booking the landing slot at take-off, or holding aircraft on the ground until a stand is reserved, beat the first-come rule?
r: Yes where pads are scarce: with 2 pads per site and 3 requests an hour each way, the first-come rule never meets the service and reserve criterion at any stand count up to 16, booking the slot at take-off needs 8 stands per site and waiting on the ground for a stand needs 5, at the price of longer passenger waits (about 225-285 s against 46-130 s). With 4 pads the rules converge. Two pads run out before stands do from 6 requests an hour in DFW and 12 in Houston. One prediction failed (aircraft left waiting at the end of the run, which were ordinary queueing, not a deadlock).

name: How wide are the air-taxi headlines? (UNCERT1)
q: Draw the uncertain inputs from stated ranges and see how far the headline numbers move
r: The share of jobs saving 10+ minutes by flying becomes 1.2 % in DFW (5th-95th: 0.02-4.9 %) and 0.5 % in Houston (0.2-2.4 %), against the 3.1 % and 1.3 % of the single-point run: that point was optimistic. What matters most is how fast the road is that people would otherwise drive, then pad processing time. The required fleet is robust (DFW at 3 flights an hour each way: 12-16 aircraft; Houston 8-12) and moves mainly with the charging rate. The ranges are my assumptions. One prediction failed (which input matters most for the access share).

name: Amazon anywhere in its Texas band (AMZBAND)
q: Fly Amazon at heights drawn across its filed 55–115 m band
r: Sharing out still cuts 75 %; Amazon–Zipline remains the biggest pair.

name: Where people live, Richardson (RICHPOP)
q: Do Census-placed customers explain how often drones pass over one Richardson street?
r: No: they lower the share (0.8× of uniform, prediction failed). A known no-fly zone explains about a fifth; the rest is unexplained (see CORRIDOR).

name: Common return height, Amazon high return (RTHREP)
q: Does the common-return-height result depend on where Amazon flies?
r: No: a common 120 m return is 8.6× worse than each drone's own height (10.7× under the allocation). One prediction failed: the rate was slightly lower than under the allocation.

name: Amazon best-sourced heights, DFW (AMZSRC_DFW)
q: Same as AMZSRC with Amazon's DFW sites
r: Sharing out cuts 66–71 % (3 runs; the 10-run headline gives 73 %); Amazon–Zipline is 79 % of what remains.

name: Meetings at a company's own sites (SITECAP)
q: How do a site's own drones meet near it as traffic grows?
r: Roughly with the square of its traffic; pads 120 m apart cut them 75–83 % at 4× traffic; spacing departures alone cannot reach 80 %.

name: Time slots at sites (ARRIVE)
q: Do arrival and departure slots remove near-site meetings?
r: Barely (−1 % to 53 %); spreading pads does. 3 of 4 predictions failed; partly superseded by PADS.

name: Air taxi against the peak-hour car (AIRTAXI_NET1)
q: How much time to get to and from the pads can an air taxi spend and still beat the peak car on six Texas routes?
r: 20.0–44.5 minutes (average of both directions and both peaks, including check-in, with no queueing; one route ties at 20). Fleet at 1.5 requests an hour per route direction: 8 (DFW), 6 (Houston; 5 after the v2 engine fix). One prediction failed (fleet growth at high demand, traced to an engine flaw fixed in v2).

name: Pads per air-taxi site (AIRTAXI_NET2)
q: How many landing pads does each site need as demand grows?
r: 2 pads cope at low demand; DFW needs 4 at 6 requests an hour per route direction and more than 4 at 12; a 3-minute pad time roughly doubles the pads. 8 of 14 predictions failed (I expected one pad to be enough at low demand). Parking stands unlimited here; see STANDS1 and PADRULE1.

name: Battery reserve and holding energy (AIRTAXI_NET3)
q: Do NET2's fleets survive when holding burns battery and a 20-minute reserve applies (FAA powered-lift rule as reported)?
r: Yes, if 100 km stay usable after the reserve. With a 130 km battery and a 20-minute reserve three of the six routes cannot be flown. Long holds in overloaded cases mean infeasible runs, not just delays.

name: Air-taxi noise on the ground (AIRTAXI_NOISE1)
q: How loud would these networks be for people near the sites?
r: Highest day-night level off-site 54 dB over 12 daytime hours (no evening or night flights), under the FAA's 65; 55 dBA events reach about 2.4 km (4.4 km if the aircraft are 5 dB louder). One prediction failed (event counts 1 km out).

name: Break-even on engine v5 and Archer's 12-site network (AIRTAXI_NET4)
q: Does break-even survive the engine fixes, and how big a fleet does Archer's announced network need with commute-shaped demand?
r: Archer's DFW network needs about 12 / 18 / 36 aircraft at 12 / 24 / 48 trips an hour, more than the 7-site network. In Houston at 100 km usable range the Galveston links to IAH and Sugar Land cannot be flown (30 % of demand). The registered break-even check failed because I gave an oversized fleet too few stands; with unlimited stands (exploratory) break-even is unchanged.

name: Power each air-taxi site would draw (AIRTAXI_POWER1)
q: Peak power and daily energy per site, compared with the NREL/FAA vertiport study
r: Busiest site about 0.6-1.1 MW at 24 trips an hour and 0.9-2.1 MW at 48, depending on energy per km (0.45-0.85 kWh): above NREL's constrained 900 kW per site, far below its unconstrained 13.3 MW.

name: People under the air-taxi noise, evenings and nights (AIRTAXI_NOISE2)
q: How many people live under the noise footprint, and what do evening and night flights add to the day-night level?
r: Nobody off-site reaches DNL 65 even with flights to midnight (highest 56.8 dB) and nobody lives where it reaches 55; about 7,600 people (DFW) and 2,100 (Houston) would hear 10+ loud flights a day at the middle level. Later hours add under 1 dB to 22:00 and 2.4-3.3 dB to midnight, slightly outside my predicted bands; counts are lumpy (one large Census block).

name: Departure corridors for all three companies (CORR2)
q: Does the headline cut in planned conflicts survive when Amazon, Wing and Zipline all fly departure corridors instead of straight routes?
r: Yes. Sharing out heights still cuts planned conflicts by 71% in Houston and 82% in DFW against best-sourced Amazon (straight routes: 72% and 73%). Corridors raise current-practice conflicts a little (1.09x Houston, 1.29x DFW). DFW's cut is 9 points above its straight-route cut, near the edge of the registered band.

name: Plan-sharing cost with ten runs (SEEDS2)
q: Does the realistic plan-sharing cost hold with 10 windy hours instead of 3?
r: Yes. With shared heights about 19% of flights in Houston and 17.5% in DFW wait (1 in 5 and 1 in 6), about 6 minutes each; current heights delay about twice as many (39% and 37%). Plan sharing removes 99-99.6% of flown planned conflicts.

name: Filed caps on overlapping service areas (CAPS1)
q: Does the headline survive when the filed daily caps on overlapping service areas are applied?
r: The relative result mostly survives: shared heights cut planned conflicts by 72% in Houston (same as uncapped) and 59% in DFW (73% uncapped). Absolute conflict counts fall by about 90% (Houston) and 82% (DFW), so every absolute count on the pages is an upper bound. With caps, 94-97% of remaining conflicts involve Amazon.

name: Real weather in the flying day (WX1)
q: How much of the daytime would rain or strong gusts take away, and were the windy test hours dry?
r: In 2025, 22% (Houston) and 13% (DFW) of daytime hours had measurable rain, 12% and 16% had 10 m gusts of 40 km/h or more, and 4-5% met a heavy-rain or 55 km/h gust label. The data cannot see thunderstorms (zero in both files), so that share is a lower bound. The windy test hours were mostly dry (2 of 10 wet).

name: Air-taxi close approaches in the air (AIRTAXI_ENC1)
q: With no steering and one cruise height, how often do air taxis come close enough that a controller would have to separate them, and does one height per direction fix it?
r: Often: at the middle level about 27 an hour in DFW and 13 in Houston come within 1.5 NM and 500 ft (en route plus near sites), growing with about the square of traffic. One height per direction removes about two thirds of the en-route ones, not the 80% predicted, because aircraft still climb and descend through the other height near sites; near sites it does not help.

name: Air taxi on a flown path 15% longer than the straight line (AIRTAXI_ROUTE1)
q: Straight-line flight time was used while battery use already assumed a path 15% longer. How much do break-even times and fleets change if flight time is lengthened too?
r: Break-even access times fall by 1.0 to 1.7 minutes per route (19 to 43 minutes instead of 20 to 45); the route order, the Alliance-Toyota-only headline at 40 minutes, and the required fleet (DFW 8, Houston 5) are unchanged. All 21 predictions passed, but they came from simple arithmetic, so this is a bookkeeping correction, not a surprise.

name: Houston area outage recounted at 4 checks per second (RECOUNT1)
q: Does the area-outage result (7.0x fewer planned conflicts with shared heights, counted once per second) hold with the finer counting used since 23 Oct?
r: Yes: 6.5x fewer (95% interval 4.9-8.8) over 10 runs at 4 checks per second; the original 3 runs give 5.3x at 4 per second. Finer counting finds more short crossings in both arms. The old count was reproduced exactly first.

name: Noise with departures into the real wind (AIRTAXI_NOISEWIND1)
q: Does taking off and landing into the real 2025 wind, instead of along the line to the next site, change who would hear the air taxis?
r: Yes: the loud-flight footprint is 2.5-3.8 times as many squares, the loudest spot is 0.3-3 dB lower, and the people hearing 10+ loud flights a day rise in 5 of 6 setups (DFW 48 trips an hour: 7,600 to 15,600). Nobody lives where the day-night level reaches 55 dB. I predicted the peak would move by under 1.5 dB everywhere; Houston's fell 2.4-3.0 dB. Five wind days per metro, lumpy census counts, the join between cruise and climb-out is not flown.

name: How well my own predictions held up (CALIB1)
q: Were my registered predictions well calibrated? Every one said "holds".
r: No: 274 of 353 held (78 %, 95 % interval 73-82 %), against an implied near-100 %. No kind of prediction did better, no improvement over time, and air-taxi questions did slightly better than drone ones, not worse. When a numeric prediction missed, the result was worse for the system than I predicted about twice as often as better (37 to 19). I predicted 5 things about my own forecasting and 1 held.

name: Does height sharing survive GPS-level errors? (ERRORS1)
q: If every drone has the published GPS-level sideways, height and late-start errors, how much of the height-sharing cut and of the plan-check benefit is left?
r: Most of the cut at best-site and average GPS (against the filed heights: 76-79 % at L1, 59-63 % at L2, from 80-81 % without errors; the 72/73 % headline case was not rerun), but only 20-30 % at the worst committed site and at the Remote ID rule size; height error alone does nearly all the damage, sideways error and late start almost none. The minimal plan check removes 77-83 % of flown conflicts at average GPS and 18-22 % at the Remote ID size; a block taller than the error holds at nearly twice the waiting flights. I predicted a lower cut at L2-L4 (3 misses). Errors are independent between flights, which likely overstates the damage; late-start size is assumed.

name: Collision risk per flight hour (RISK1)
q: How does height sharing change modelled collision risk per flight hour, rather than plan overlaps, under GPS-level errors?
r: It cuts modelled collision risk about as much as planned conflicts: 79 % (Houston) and 82 % (DFW) at best-site GPS, 61 % and 58 % at average GPS, 78-83 % at average GPS if most of the error is shared by nearby drones, and at least 16-18 % at the Remote ID size. All 5 predictions held. No plan check or avoidance is modelled, so the rates (about 1 per 10,000 flight hours) describe uncoordinated plans; Zipline and Amazon sizes are assumed.

name: In-flight avoidance (AVOID1)
q: If drones detect each other through Remote ID and climb or descend away, how much modelled collision risk is left, and does height sharing still matter?
r: At exact GPS avoidance removes up to 71 % of modelled collision risk (its success rate), but at the GPS standard's average error only 3-5 %: most of that risk comes from drones planned more than 10 m apart in height that their errors bring together, which Remote ID broadcasts cannot show, and a 10 m target gap is inside the height error. Height sharing still cuts the remaining risk by 57-61 % and manoeuvres by three quarters. I predicted a 50-71 % cut (2 misses).

name: The headline case under errors, and errors shared by nearby drones (ERRORS2)
q: Does the 72-73 % headline cut survive GPS-level errors, and what if most of the error is shared by nearby drones, as GPS and barometer physics suggests?
r: Independent errors shrink the headline cut as in ERRORS1 (71-73 % at best-site GPS, 54-60 % at average GPS, 22-23 % at the Remote ID size). If 80-95 % of the error is shared by nearby drones, the average-GPS cut is 66-75 %, close to the no-error 72-74 %: only each drone's personal error matters (shared plus personal gives the same cut as personal alone). All 10 predictions held, some with wide bands. How much is shared on real drones is not measured.

name: Collision risk with the plan check on (RISK2)
q: Once flight plans are checked against each other before take-off, how much modelled collision risk is left, and does height sharing still lower it?
r: The minimal check removes 81-96 % of modelled collision risk at average GPS (all of it at best-site GPS); the larger one removes all of it but delays 40-48 % of flights and cancels about 26 %. With the minimal check the shared-out heights keep more residual risk than Amazon's best-sourced heights (Houston 0.93 vs 0.82, DFW 1.11 vs 0.51 per 100,000 flight hours), because their Amazon and Zipline layers are exactly 20 m apart, the edge of what the check sees. Height sharing still halves the flights delayed. 3 of 5 predictions failed.

name: Worse GPS downtown and drifting errors (ERRORS3)
q: Does poor GPS among tall buildings change the modelled collision risk, and does it break the plan check if it applies everywhere?
r: Urban-canyon sideways error downtown only changes metro-wide modelled risk by +0.1 %, because under 0.4 % of close encounters are downtown (0.1-0.3 % in DFW, 0.3 % in Houston). With canyon error everywhere, risk without a check changes by at most 6 %. I predicted the residual risk with the minimal plan check would rise by at least 50 %; it changed by -11 % to +17 %, so that prediction failed. Errors that drift during a flight were settled by argument, not runs. 1 of 4 predictions failed.

name: Weather stops and catch-up afterwards (WX2)
q: If drones stop in bad weather and catch up afterwards, what happens to conflicts over a year?
r: Stops plus catch-up at up to 1.5x add about 6-7 % to a year's planned conflicts (9 % at up to 2x), because conflicts grow roughly with the square of traffic (exponent 1.98-2.09). Height sharing keeps its 72-75 % cut at double traffic. I predicted the plan check would delay a much larger share of flights at double traffic; the delayed share barely moved while cancellations rose, so that failed.

name: Deliveries bunched at lunch and dinner (DEMAND1)
q: If deliveries peak at lunch and dinner instead of spreading evenly, how many more conflicts are there?
r: With the busiest hour twice the day's average (same daily total), a day's planned conflicts rise 40-48 % and the busiest hour has about 4 times the conflicts of an even hour. Houston came in above my predicted 15-45 % range. Height sharing keeps its cut. The demand shape is from food delivery in Beijing; drone demand is not published.

name: Real helicopter traffic against the drone layers (HELI1)
q: Where do real helicopters in Houston and Dallas-Fort Worth fly relative to the drone layers, and how much drone traffic would they meet?
r: Across 14 days of 2025 tracks, 30 % (Houston) and 46 % (DFW) of helicopter time in the counted areas is below 150 m above ground and 14-17 % is inside the drone height band, far more than I predicted (under 15 % and under 8 %); the shares depend a lot on the assumed ground elevation (roughly 20-60 %). On average a low-flying helicopter has 0.03 (Houston) or 0.009 (DFW) drones in a 450 x 450 x 60 m box around it, and height sharing does not change that. Volunteer receivers miss low flights, so these are floors. 3 of 5 predictions failed.
